title: Sharp universal death of entanglement threshold for Pauli Hamiltonians
abstract: We determine the exact universal high-temperature separability threshold for Pauli Hamiltonians of bounded degree $Δ\ge2$. If every coefficient in the Hamiltonian has magnitude at most one and each term has overlapping support with at most $Δ$ other terms, the Gibbs state is a mixture of product Pauli eigenstates whenever \[   β\le z_Δ:= \operatorname{arctanh}\left[\max_{0\le x \le 1}x\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right)^{Δ-1} \right]. \] For every $β>z_Δ$, a finite commuting Hamiltonian with maximum overlap degree at most $Δ$ has an entangled Gibbs state. At any fixed $β<z_Δ$ strictly below the threshold, a classical polynomial-time algorithm produces samples from a distribution over product Pauli eigenstates approximating the Gibbs state in trace distance.
summary: This work precisely calculates the critical inverse temperature ($ eta$) at which the Gibbs state of a Pauli Hamiltonian transitions from being separable (product state mixture) to entangled. The threshold, $z_\Delta$, depends universally on the maximum degree ($\Delta$) of the Hamiltonian's term-overlap graph. This provides a powerful tool for understanding thermal decoherence and entanglement decay in quantum many-body systems.
main_problem: The paper determines the exact universal high-temperature separability threshold for Gibbs states generated by Pauli Hamiltonians.
main_result: A sharp threshold $z_\Delta$ is established: the Gibbs state is separable if the inverse temperature $ eta$ is below $z_\Delta$, and entangled otherwise.
method: The proof uses inclusion-exclusion formulas and graph theory arguments applied to the term-overlap graph structure of the Hamiltonian.

key_observables: Separability of the Gibbs state, the inverse temperature $ eta$, and the threshold $z_\Delta$.

main_assumptions: The analysis often focuses on the structure of the term-overlap graph, particularly when it is a tree, to derive the sharpest threshold.

paper_structure: The paper develops the threshold determination using decomposition techniques (inclusion-exclusion) to establish the separability criterion, followed by detailed analysis on the structure of the graph to find the critical temperature $z_\Delta$, and concludes with efficient sampling algorithms for the separable regime.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, quantitative threshold for when quantum correlations (entanglement) are expected to vanish in thermal equilibrium for local Hamiltonians, which is crucial for understanding quantum phase transitions in many-body systems.
